newsitem.title: MALI: Mali opposition calls for fresh elections.
newsitem.headline: Mali opposition calls for fresh elections.

text.p: Opposition parties in Mali have called for the West African nation's second multi-party elections to be suspended and reorganised following chaotic weekend parliamentary polls.

Mountaga Tall, head of the leading National Congress of the Democratic Initiative CNID party, said 11 parties in two opposition groups also demanded President Alpha Oumar Konare's government quit for failing to arrange proper polling.
"We have decided not to recognise the results of the election of April 13," Tall told Radio France International in an interview broadcast on Tuesday.
"We have decided to demand...the suspension of the electoral process, that is round two of the parliamentary election and the presidential and municipal elections."
The two opposition alliances also demand the dissolution of the Independent National Electoral Commission, set up in January at their demand by Konare, and an audit of its activities.

Sunday's poll for a new 147-seat national assembly and presidential and municipal elections in May and June are a test of how deeply democracy has taken root in Mali, which won widespread praise for its 1992 democratic transition.
A total 1,500 candidates from 21 parties contested the election, notably supporters of Konare, a historian elected in 1992, and candidates from the two main opposition alliances.

Voters flocked to polling stations for the election, which launched the impoverished nation's second multi-party national polls since independence from France in 1960, only to find that organisational glitches prevented them voting.
They cited problems with voter cards and electotal lists and lack of voting materials.

Early results from six towns, released by the CENI on Monday, suggested Konare's ruling ADEMA alliance enjoyed an early lead but in all but one town, its party lists failed to achieve the outright majority needed to win seats.
The second round has been set for April 27.
Turnout in the 1992 parliamentary poll was little more than 20 percent. Sunday's early turnout raised hopes of a turnout of 40 to 50 percent, but enthusiasm waned as problems persisted.
The opposition Front for Change and Democracy (FCD) and the Rally of Patriotic Forces (RFP) had denounced preparations for the elections before the poll.
The RFP, of which Tall's party is a part, includes supporters of the former single party and jailed former dictator Moussa Traore, whose 1991 overthrow cleared the way for democratic reform.
The FCD portrays itself as heir to the tradition of independence leader Modibo Keita, a nationalist and hardline socialist who declared a one-party state after independence.
Konare faces nine challengers in a May 4 presidential poll. He has steered Mali on a course of economic liberalisation, winning praise from the United States and the World Bank.
Landlocked on the edge of the Sahara desert, Mali has few natural advantages apart from gold -- a sector it is expanding.
